name: Executive order of September 9, 1873 defining the Port Madison Reservation (Treaty of Point Elliott)
promises: Royce records an 1873 order on this reserve as made simply to cure the indefinite language of the Treaty of Point Elliott of January 22, 1855, which set apart the Port Madison reserve.
The Suquamish Tribe states that the Treaty of Point Elliott provided that the Port Madison Indian Reservation be held in trust for the tribe by the federal government.

breaches.what: The Suquamish Tribe states that after allotment much reservation land was sold without the owners' consent by federal agents who declared owners non-competent under a 1907 act, that later certificates of competency removed land from trust, and that many members lost land for state taxes they could not pay.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Suquamish Tribe, History and Culture page

today: The Suquamish Tribe states that a large share of reservation land is owned by non-Indian residents and that buying land back on the reservation is a major tribal goal.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says it was forced onto individual allotments in 1904 after the destruction of Old Man House in 1870, and that allotted land was then lost through sales by federal agents without owners' consent, competency certificates and state taxes.

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule p. 864

openQuestions: This Royce record (area 349) is an executive order defining an existing treaty reserve, not a cession; the Point Elliott treaty has its own record. Matching Royce's note "to cure the indefinite language of the treaty" to the September 9, 1873 date rests on the scanned schedule, whose columns are jumbled.

No court or Indian Claims Commission finding on the loss of Port Madison land was located; the Commission's Suquamish case concerns the Point Elliott cession. Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe (1978) concerns criminal jurisdiction, not land, and was not used.
The Duwamish Tribe is not federally recognized and was not researched for this order; most Duwamish did not move to Port Madison.
The order's text was not opened.

plain.promised: An 1873 order fixed the bounds of the Port Madison Reservation set apart by the 1855 Point Elliott treaty, which the Suquamish Tribe says was to be held in trust for the tribe.
plain.happened: The Suquamish Tribe says federal agents sold allotted land without owners' consent and state taxes took more. No court or commission finding was located.
plain.today: The Tribe says much of the reservation is owned by non-Indians and it is buying land back.
